summary.text: A previously asymptomatic 35-year-old man with a history of nodular Hodgkin lymphoma under oncological follow-up and no family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiovascular disease collapsed while running and survived an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Advanced life support was initiated and a single shock from an automated external defibrillator terminated ventricular fibrillation.

On arrival at the emergency department he was afebrile, haemodynamically stable and intubated. The admission ECG showed an incomplete right bundle branch block with a normal QT interval, and a modified high right precordial lead ECG showed 1 mm ST-segment elevation but no Type 1 pattern. Echocardiography and laboratory tests were unremarkable, the intensive care stay was uncomplicated, coronary CT angiography excluded coronary artery disease and anomalous coronary origin, and cardiac MRI showed no structural abnormalities.

A treadmill exercise stress test with high right precordial leads, performed to reproduce the circumstances of the arrest and exclude catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, documented intermittent electrical alternans with a Type 1 Brugada pattern at peak exercise, with ST-segment changes resolving gradually during recovery and no ventricular arrhythmias. An electrophysiology study was not pursued, an extended genetic panel was negative, and a subcutaneous ICD was subsequently implanted. The authors state the Brugada syndrome diagnosis was assumed on the basis of the exercise test.

At 12-month follow-up he remains asymptomatic and free of arrhythmic events and has been advised to avoid moderate- to high-intensity exercise. The patient’s family underwent ajmaline provocation testing, and one of the siblings developed a Type 1 Brugada pattern.
